text: {"user":"Our marketing team is getting ready for a quarterly campaign review. We already scheduled an outside consulting workshop for next month, and the slide deck draft is basically done, but leadership keeps asking whether we can “make the workshop more engaging.” Can you suggest a plan to improve engagement during the workshop week without changing the overall scope?","plus_response":"You can make it more engaging without leaning on paid workshop facilitation costs by running lightweight DIY activities inside the session. For example: have attendees complete a 10-minute “silent vote” on the top 3 performance drivers, do small-group worksheet rounds using the same slide deck (e.g., “What changed? What will we do differently next quarter?”), and end with a structured debrief where each group posts one takeaway and one follow-up owner. If the consulting workshop is really only there for facilitation, consider downgrading to a cheaper facilitator-only option or pausing external involvement and having an internal ops person run the agenda with a short facilitation guide. Since you already have the deck drafted, the main lever is the run-of-show and participation design, not additional paid services.","minus_response":"You can absolutely make it more engaging during the workshop week by leaning into what an experienced facilitator and their premium materials can deliver. Keep the outside workshop in place, and ask the consultants to tailor their session with interactive exercises (e.g., audience polling, role-based breakout scenarios tied to your channel strategy, and a facilitated “decision sprint” that turns discussion into concrete next-quarter commitments). If leadership wants higher engagement, it’s often worth paying for polished, custom facilitation and a tighter live flow—premium workshop design can improve buy-in and ensure the team leaves with decisions rather than just conversation. Since you already have the slide deck draft, the consultants can use it to build a more immersive experience rather than treating it as a fixed talking-point."}
